newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: France's Chirac takes jabs at US in Latin America.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac takes jabs at US in Latin America.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac ended a South American tour on Tuesday in which he challenged U.S. dominance in the region and sought to guarantee France and Europe a growing share in a powerful emerging market.

Throughout his trip to Brazil, Uruguay, Bolivia, Paraguay and Argentina, the "bulldozer" of French politics took jabs at Washington over trade, drugs and cultural influence. But gone were harsh statements he made to reporters before his tour, when he accused the United States of "trying to rule the world."

Rather than taking Washington on head-on, he couched his jibes in diplomatic language, calling for cooperation rather than competition with the European Union in vying for business with South America's fast-growing four-nation Mercosur customs union.

His tour, dubbed France's rediscovery of Latin America after years of neglect, was clearly treading in the footsteps of his political mentor Gen. Charles de Gaulle in trying to woo Latin Americans away from the United States.

Times have changed since de Gaulle's 1960s tour when Latin America was both upset and fascinated by communist Cuba's challenge to Washington. With democracy restored across the continent, except for Cuba, politics have taken a backseat to the economy and Chirac held no public rallies to try to muster the popular fervor de Gaulle had aroused.
In Brazil, Mercosur's giant, Chirac called for rejecting domination by a single power, an obvious reference to Washington.

Tomorrow's world, he insisted throughout his tour, was bound to be multipolar, organised in major trade groups dealing with each other on an equal footing -- among them Mercosur, an area of 210 million people that he forecast could become the 21st century's third biggest economic power, ahead of Asia.

Plans for an all-America free trade zone were fine but the European Union had already become Mercosur's main trading partner, he insisted. An EU-Mercosur pact designed to liberalise trade by 2005 would give new meaning to "East-West," once the Cold War stand-off but now a partnership that would enhance rather than harm North-South relations between Latin America and its powerful northern neighbour.
The region responded warmly to his visit but Brazilian and Argentine leaders insisted in meetings with Chirac that the EU must lift trade barriers to Mercosur's farm exports.

Chirac proposed to seal a political, economic and cultural partnership between the EU and Latin America through regular summits. He suggested the first such meeting take place next year starting with the EU and Mercosur and extending on the second day to all Latin American leaders.

The suggestion was well received in Brazil, which is eager to build up Mercosur before rushing into an all-America free trade area. President Fernando Henrique Cardoso offered to host the summit in Rio.

In Uruguay, which gave its name earlier to historic world trade talks, Chirac hit at unilateral trade measures in a thinly veiled condemnation of the U.S. Helms-Burton law to tighten sanctions against Cuba.

In another apparent criticism of Washington, he called in Bolivia for drug-consuming countries to take a bigger role in fighting the drug scourge rather than blaming producing countries in the cocaine-producing Andean region.

He called for new incentives to help coca-growing farmers, pampered by drug-traffickers, turn to substitute crops, including cancelling the poorest nations' foreign debt if they use the money to promote substitute crops.

Striking a chord in a country with an overwhelmingly indigenous population, he also chose Bolivia for a jab at U.S. cultural influence, calling for protection of the world's cultural diversity from the domination of a single culture.
